title: Storefront: A Century of Small Businesses | Urban Archive
text:
Storefront: A Century of Small Businesses | Urban Archive

By 

New York City’s small businesses have always reflected the personality of our neighborhoods, serving the needs of their neighbors, near and far. From bakeries and bars to grocery stores and pharmacies, they showcase the vital role that local retail plays in creating a livable city. Behind each storefront is a story of family and immigrant-owned business, an unsung workforce, and generations of love for the city.

While we are being asked to limit our trips out of the house, let’s take a look back at the small businesses that have kept New York City humming through good times and bad. #NoSmallBizNoNY

## Grace Church

Fleischmann’s Vienna Model Bakery, Broadway and 10th Street, 1898.

Sometime after 1876, Louis Fleischmann built his bakery on Broadway, in the shadow on James Renwick’s Grace Church (left). The bakery, which sold a popular “new dough” style of bread made with yeast, also operated a restaurant and rented storefront space to other vendors.

## Cavanagh's Restaurant 

1905

Cavanagh’s Restaurant ca. 1905 Irish pubs and taverns, some serving restaurant food, were central features of New York City Irish neighborhoods.

## Park & Tilford Building 

1908

Park and Tilford was one of New York’s most prestigious purveyors of fine spirits, choice groceries, and tobacco. The rich of Harlem shopped here in the 1910s, and a teenage Henry Roth (later to become an acclaimed writer) worked as a delivery boy. Delivering groceries throughout the neighborhood, he observed that Harlem was a divided community: white gentiles shopped primarily on 125th Street, Jews on 116th Street, and African Americans on 135th Street.

## Meyerrose House

1910

Meyerrose House, ca. 1910.

Constructed in 1906 for Joseph Meyerrose, a well-known Ridgewood political figure and Queens County Sheriff, the blonde brick and terra cotta building, still stands! The Meyerrose family, one of the founding Ridgewood families, occupied the home until 1920. In 1922 they sold the building to the Queens Labor Lyceum, a social club for the unionized residents, the majority of whom worked in local breweries. The social club offered public lectures, concerts, civic events, and a restaurant. The building served as a knitting mill in the 1970s and 1980s. Today it is Descent of the Holy Spirit Romanian Orthodox Church.

## 5820 Broadway

5820 Broadway, circa 1915. Most of the oldest bars in New York City are in lower Manhattan, but the Bronx has its own century-old bar in Kingsbridge.

## 1881 Park Avenue

1921

Gristede Brothers, ca. 1921. Founded by two teenage brothers, Diedrich (Dick) and Charles Gristede, in 1888, Gristede’s would become a city mainstay over the next half century. The original small grocery store, located at 42nd Street and 2nd Avenue, prospered and within 50 years the grocery store had become a successful chain with more than 150 stores in the city, Westchester, Long Island and Connecticut. This 128th Street location opened in a new purpose-built structure in 1920. Today the building still stands, sans the ‘Gristede Brothers 1920’ lettering that once graced the triangular pediment at the top.

## Old Farrington Hall

Farrington Hall Storefronts on Broadway. The large building in the center is the former Farrington Hall. Signs on the exterior advertise auto supplies.
